title: The different worlds of Google – A comparison of search results on conspiracy theories in 12 countries
screen_reason: Comparative content analysis of 1,259 temporally stable first-page Google results for 11 popular conspiracy theories in 12 countries and 10 languages. Every link was double-coded as conspiratorial (CT-confirming), debunking or neutral, and Table 2 gives the share of CT-confirming results per country (5% to 30%) with per-country denominators. That is a share of items in a sample coded false/misleading against researcher judgement, i.e. CONTENT.

estimates.country: 12 countries: Australia, Brazil, Czech Republic, Germany, Ghana, Hungary, Italy, Poland, Romania, Serbia, Switzerland, Ukraine (10 languages)
estimates.platform: Google Search (organic first-page results, including results appearing in a video box)
estimates.measure_type: % of first-page Google results for 11 popular conspiracy theories that were coded as CT-confirming (all 12 countries pooled)
estimates.value_raw: Table 2 column totals: Confirming N = 187 of N = 1259 temporally stable URLs (187/1259 = 14.9%); other columns: debunking 413, neutral-descriptive 311, satirical 40, related 167, unrelated 106, unclear 35
estimates.denominator: 1,259 temporally stable first-page Google URLs, pooled across 11 conspiracy theories x 12 countries (per-country n from 71 in Brazil to 115 in Czech Republic and Hungary)
estimates.definition: A link entered the numerator if the content of the page it pointed to was coded as conspiratorial, i.e. CONFIRMING the conspiracy theory searched for. Debunking content and neutral content (descriptive without confirming or denying, satirical, topic-related but not the CT, or wholly unrelated) were excluded from the numerator, as was an 'unclear' residual category.
estimates.misinfo_def: Conspiracy theories are defined as explanations of ‘important events as secret plots by government or powerful individuals’ (Kapantai et al., 2021: 1325) that ‘contradict the general consensus among epistemic authorities’ (Brotherton and Eser, 2015: 1); links were coded as CT ‘conspiratorial’ (confirming), ‘debunking’ or ‘neutral’
estimates.source_quote: We analysed links from Google search results (N = 1259) in 12 Western and non-Western countries and 10 languages. Overall, users are more likely to encounter neutral or debunking content when using Google to search for prominent CTs.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract (quoted); column totals in Table 2 final row, p. 2276 (Confirming N = 187 of N = 1259)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Manual content analysis by native-speaker researchers using a shared codebook; each link double-coded for content stance with Krippendorff's alpha mean 0.88 (minimum 0.82) and for source type with alpha mean 0.92 (minimum 0.83). No external fact-checker or domain list: the coders judged each page against the CT it was retrieved for.
estimates.moderator_quote: We analysed temporally stable URLs (N = 1259) in two categories in keeping with the setup of Ballatore’s study (2015) (see codebook in the supplement): First, we determined the source type of each link (Krippendorff’s alpha mean= 0.92, min = 0.83 [...]). Second, we recorded the content of the pages was conspiratorial, debunking or neutral (alpha mean= 0.88, min = 0.82). || To avoid personalisation effects, we made sure that users were not logged into Google when they conducted their search; that the local language was selected in the search settings; and that search customisation was disabled [...] We limited our collection of search results to the first Google results page, since users rarely take note of hits on the second page (Jansen and Spink, 2006). [...] we conducted our searches on 10 consecutive days in August/September 2021. Our final sample only included URLs that appeared on the first results page on at least 5 days.
estimates.notes: POOLED ROW, DERIVED VALUE: the paper prints no overall percentage, only the Table 2 column count N = 187 against the stated total N = 1259, so 14.9% is an exact part/whole share from verbatim counts over the same base (R8). Cross-check: weighting the 12 verbatim country percentages by their link counts recovers 187.7 confirming links, consistent with the printed 187. The 12 country rows below decompose this figure - do NOT pool the pooled row together with the country rows. Pooling is unweighted by population or search volume: it is a mean over an artificial design of 11 CTs x 12 countries, so it describes the study design, not any real population's search experience. QUOTE NOTE: the Table 2 total row is transposed in the plain-text extraction, so the contiguous Abstract sentence stating N = 1259 and the overall direction is quoted; the counts behind the value are in value_raw.

(1) PER-CONSPIRACY-THEORY shares (RQ1a, Figure 1 and supplementary Table S4, which is not in this text): only fragments are stated in prose, most of them imprecise ('up to', 'more than half', 'at most'). The clean ones are: QAnon 0% confirming in every country; Pizzagate 8% confirmatory overall, but 40% in Serbia; Vaccination Damage 10% in the Czech Republic, Poland, Ukraine and Switzerland; Flat Earth at most 25% (Ghana); Climate Change Hoax up to 38% (Serbia), with Australia, Brazil and Italy above 20%; 9/11 36% (Czech Republic) and 44% (Hungary); Directed Energy Weapons 10% (Germany, Hungary) to more than half (Ukraine, Italy); Reptilians average 30%, up to 73% (Czech Republic and Romania); Depopulation Agenda average 28%, more than half (Romania, Serbia, Poland). These are CT x country cells; extracting them would mean dozens of rows, most without a stated denominator, so per R4 they are left here. The Reptilians (30%) and Depopulation Agenda (28%) cross-country averages are the most defensible additions if an adjudicator wants CT-level rows. (2) SOURCE-TYPE shares (RQ1b): mainstream media 5% CT-confirming on average (up to 12% in Ukraine and Serbia); social media more than a third on average, above 50% in Serbia, Romania and Italy and 12% in Germany, Ghana and 'Austria'; alternative media 64% on average; e-commerce up to 36%; public service media 0%; fact-checking, academic and government sites confirming only in Ukraine, Ghana and Italy. These are source-type subgroups within the same 1,259 links, not the paper's headline denominator. NOTE the typo for an adjudicator: the text lists 'Austria' among the low-social-media-confirming countries, but Austria is not in the sample - Australia is meant. (3) Source-type COMPOSITION shares (mainstream media 33% of links on average, 45% in Brazil, 23% in Ukraine and Ghana; social media 9%; cyclopedias/Wikipedia 11%) describe the mix of sources, not falsity. (4) Ballatore's (2015) figures quoted in the literature review and Discussion (48.4% of Google result pages conspiratorial, 14.1% neutral, 33.1% debunking) are cited from another study and are excluded by R8. (5) The debunking, neutral and unclear columns of Table 2 are the non-misinformation complement of the extracted rows. (6) The dominance analysis (source type explains 67% of the pseudo-R2 of 0.37, CT topic 21%, country 12%) and the RQ2 correlations (Democracy Index r = 0.68, CPI r = 0.65, Press Freedom r = 0.64, GDP r = 0.42, media trust r = 0.3, polarisation r = 0.12) are associations, not prevalence. (7) topic is coded 'other' on every row because the 11 CTs deliberately mix domains (health/vaccines, climate and other science, 9/11 and political conspiracies, plus Reptilians and Illuminati); no single topic code fits the basket, and the per-CT breakdown that would allow finer coding is in the unavailable supplement.

rob.design: Cross-national search-engine content analysis, no human participants. Eleven conspiracy theories (the 10 most shared on Twitter per Mahl et al. 2021, plus QAnon) were searched on Google in 12 countries (Australia, Brazil, Czech Republic, Germany, Ghana, Hungary, Italy, Poland, Romania, Serbia, Switzerland, Ukraine) and 10 languages, with search terms translated and localised by native-speaker researchers. Searches were run from desktop computers physically located in each country, not logged in, with local language set and search customisation disabled; only organic first-page results (including a video box) were saved; spatial personalisation was deliberately NOT controlled because country differences are the object of study. To damp temporal volatility (about 10% of results changed day to day) searches ran on 10 consecutive days in August/September 2021 and only URLs present on page 1 on at least 5 days were kept, giving N = 1,259 URLs (71-115 per country). Each URL was coded for source type (Krippendorff's alpha mean 0.92, min 0.83) and content stance - conspiratorial, debunking or neutral (alpha mean 0.88, min 0.82). Exceptions: Italy's 10 days were non-consecutive and some Italian queries were run from the UK over a VPN. Author-stated limitations: the CT list came from a purposive English-language Twitter sample and may travel unevenly across countries; translation of queries may lose meaning; only Google, and only organic results (no news box, autocomplete or suggested searches); no structural-factor data for a systematic test, so RQ2 is exploratory with n = 12 countries.
rob.item6_quote: Second, we recorded the content of the pages was conspiratorial, debunking or neutral (alpha mean= 0.88, min = 0.82). Neutral content could a) either describe the CT without confirming or denying it, b) make fun of the CT without debunking or confirming it, c) depict a topic related to the CT, but not the CT itself (e.g. climate change, but not the CT that climate change is a hoax) or d) depict an issue completely unrelated to the CT and its topic.
rob.item10_quote: If users search for conspiracy theories, the share of CT confirming content in their search result varies significantly, depending on their country. It is lowest in Australia, Brazil, Germany and Switzerland (see Table 2), with shares below 10%, followed by Ghana and Poland at 12%.
